questions.prompt: Put the preprocessing steps in the order they are applied to continuous data on this site's path:

options.text: Re-reference to the average reference
High-pass filter at 0.1 Hz
Interpolate the removed channels
Notch filter from 58 to 62 Hz
Remove the bad channels

questions.explanation: Filtering of the continuous data comes first, then removing bad channels. The average reference comes last, because it needs all channels spread over the head: a bad channel left in spreads its noise into every channel, and a missing one tilts the average toward the other side. So interpolation comes before it.

questions.prompt: Which of these choices match the "Which value should I choose?" table in the filtering lesson? (Select all that apply)

options.text: ERP analysis: high-pass at 0.1 Hz and low-pass at 30 Hz
Computing ICA: high-pass at 1 Hz on a separate copy
Spectral analysis up to 40 Hz: low-pass at 30 Hz
An ERP with a P3: high-pass at 2 Hz to remove all drift

questions.explanation: A 30 Hz low-pass removes everything above it, so it does not suit an analysis up to 40 Hz. A 1 or 2 Hz high-pass shrinks P3 and N400 and creates opposite-polarity deflections around them, so 1 Hz is for the ICA copy only.

questions.prompt: This is the spectrum of all channels of a dataset recorded in Saudi Arabia, after a high-pass only. What causes the narrow peak, and what is the fix on this site's path?

image.alt: Spectra of all channels from 1 to 64 Hz, one line per channel, vertical axis in dB. A broad peak near 10 Hz, a gradual fall with frequency, and a sharp narrow peak at 60 Hz rising above the neighboring frequencies.
image.spec: An EEGLAB 2026.1 figure (source: eeglab-ui or script) of Plot > Channel spectra and maps on D1 hp0.1, range 1 64, **with no scalp maps** (empty maps field) so a 60 Hz map does not give the answer away. The "before" image of the line-noise lesson can be reused if drawn without maps. One version for both languages.

options.text: Line noise at 60 Hz; the fix is a notch filter from 58 to 62 Hz
Line noise at 60 Hz; the fix is a 58 to 62 Hz band-pass without the notch option
Muscle activity; the fix is a 30 Hz low-pass before ICA
An alpha peak, so no filter is needed

questions.explanation: The narrow peak at 60 Hz comes from the power grid, which runs at 60 Hz in Saudi Arabia. Without `Notch filter the data instead of pass band`, the filter becomes a band-pass that keeps only 58 to 62 Hz and removes all brain activity. A 30 Hz low-pass before ICA removes high frequencies that ICA and ICLabel need.

questions.prompt: One channel in these ten seconds is bad. Which one?

image.alt: A scroll window with channels FPz, EOG1, Fz, Cz, P4 and Oz over ten seconds. FPz and EOG1 show large, spaced peaks at the same moments in both. Channel P4 is a straight line with no variation. The other channels vary with similar amplitude.
image.spec: Script figure on an **exercise copy** of D1 hp0.1 notch60 (source: script): channels FPz, EOG1, Fz, Cz, P4 and Oz over ten seconds that contain two or three blinks, in the style of Plot > Channel data (scroll) with one shared scale. Channel P4 is set to zero in the copy (EEG.data(iP4,:) = 0) to stand for a flat electrode. Under the figure, a small English line: Simulated flat channel for this quiz. Channel names are English, so one version serves both languages.

options.text: FPz
EOG1
P4
Cz

questions.explanation: P4 is a flat line that records nothing, the clearest sign of a bad channel. The large peaks in FPz and EOG1 together are eye blinks, a normal artifact that ICA removes later, and a channel is not removed because of them. (The flat channel here is simulated for this question, because D1 has no bad channels.)

questions.prompt: Why do you interpolate removed channels before re-referencing to the average?

options.text: Because the average reference needs channels spread over the whole head, and a missing channel tilts the average toward the other side
Because interpolation adds new information to the data
Because EEGLAB refuses to re-reference when a channel is missing
Because interpolation raises the data rank

questions.explanation: An interpolated channel is a mix of its neighbors, so it adds no new information; it lowers the data rank by one. But it completes the spread of channels over the head, so the average is balanced.

questions.prompt: You re-referenced D1 to the average reference, excluding `EOG1` and `EOG2`. Which statements are true? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Every scalp channel changed shape
`EOG1` and `EOG2` stayed as they were
The data rank dropped by one, so ICA on D1 gives thirty-one components
Only the channels near the old reference changed
You can change the reference after ICA with no effect on the weights

questions.explanation: Every channel is the difference between its electrode and the reference, so changing the reference changes all channels together. Excluded channels are not part of the computation, so they stay the same. After an average reference the scalp channels sum to zero, so the rank drops by one. ICA weights are tied to the reference they were computed on, so do not change it afterward.

questions.prompt: Your data were recorded at 1000 Hz, and the highest frequency you care about is 40 Hz. Which new rate is the safe choice?

options.text: 50 Hz
64 Hz
80 Hz
250 Hz

questions.explanation: The rule: the new rate should be at least 2.5 times the highest frequency of interest, 100 Hz here. 80 Hz is only twice 40 Hz, which leaves no margin: the EEGLAB anti-aliasing filter keeps frequencies intact only up to 80% of the new Nyquist. 250 Hz is the common choice for ERP data.

questions.prompt: Your analysis is ERP only, and you will apply a 30 Hz low-pass at the end. Do you usually need a notch filter for line noise?

options.text: Yes, always, whatever the analysis
Usually not, because a 30 Hz low-pass removes the 60 Hz peak; but you need it if you keep high frequencies, as in ICA or spectral analysis
No, because line noise does not appear in ERP data
Yes, but with a wide filter from 45 to 75 Hz

questions.explanation: The decision follows the frequencies you keep. On this site's path we remove line noise even though the analysis is ERP, because we keep high frequencies until after ICA and postpone the low-pass until after cleaning. A wide filter takes real brain and muscle activity with it, so stay within ± 2 Hz.
